5: Gate 2's first step is to choose one writer per attribute, and the guide offers two patterns, as design guidance.
In the first, Entra inbound provisioning stays the door.
SailPoint aggregates H R read-only, and governs entitlements: groups, roles, access packages and application access.
In the second, SailPoint becomes the provisioning service, and takes on the duties the workbook's design gives the H R middleware.
Pick one and write it down.
Then record each attribute's writer in the program's attribute map.
One fact helps the choice: SailPoint's Oracle H C M Cloud connector reads Core H C M directly, without an on-premises appliance, and writes back only the user name and work email.

6: Step two chooses one approver system per authority class.
The guide's example, design guidance: ServiceNow approves A zero and A one through its Ask for Approval flow.
SailPoint approves A two and A three, through access-request approvals by an owner, a manager or a governance group.
The Service Catalog app only collects A two and A three requests.
And every approval's timeout outcome is reject or cancel, never approve.
Step three gives each change class a lane, following the workbook's design.
The mapping onto these products is the program's inference.
An autonomous class runs as a standard change, and the authorizing official accepts any class run that way.
A gated class is an access request with approval.

7: The guide names the automated check for Gate 2, built in the workbook's Chapter 08.

The implementation example planned a read-only check of the two provisioning mappings for Pass 2, and both configurations export as jay-son through documented reads, so the check runs on files, offline, today.
The first is the inbound job's synchronization schema, from Microsoft Graph.
It takes the rules that target the Entra directory, the enabled mappings to User, and each attribute's flow type: Always updates it on every change, and Object Add Only sets it only at creation.
The second is the SailPoint source's provisioning policies.
An Update policy is used for attribute sync, a Create policy when the account is made, and other usage types are ignored.
8: For each attribute both systems write, the check gives one of three results.
A Finding when both update it: each overwrites the other, and the command exits one.
A Warn when one updates it and the other sets it at creation: two sources for its first value.
And Info when both set it only at creation.
SailPoint's field names are the connector's, not necessarily Entra I D's.
The check matches names case-insensitively, and takes an alias for each pair that differs.
Which connector field writes which Entra attribute is something to confirm in the source's schema.
A wrong name would make every attribute look unwritten, so the check refuses a name the schema doesn't target.
9: Here's what the check guards against, from Chapter 08's dangers table.
Two systems updating one attribute means drift that's fixed and recreated on every sync, forever; that's a Finding, and an exit code of one.
Field names that differ can hide a second writer, so the check would report no overlap; the guard is the reviewed alias list.
A wrong directory name makes every attribute look unwritten; the check refuses it.
A disabled mapping counted would give false findings, so disabled object mappings are skipped.
And here's what it misses: writers outside provisioning policies.
A person has to confirm those.
The guide is clear about scope, too.
It doesn't check approver systems or lanes; those stay a manual validation of Gate 2.
